questions.question: In DSA/ECDSA, which value must be unique and secret for each signature under the same private key?
options: The public key
The signature (r,s)
The per-signature nonce k
The generator g / base point G
questions.explanation: DSA/ECDSA security depends on a fresh secret nonce k per signature; reuse or leakage can reveal the private key.

questions.question: What problem does RFC 6979 primarily address for DSA/ECDSA signing?
options: The need for high-quality randomness at signing time
The need to keep the public key secret
The need to compress signatures into fewer bytes
The need to avoid hashing the message
questions.explanation: RFC 6979 makes nonce generation deterministic from (x, H(m)), reducing dependence on an RNG during signing.

questions.question: Which relation best captures why nonce k is dangerous if reused in (EC)DSA-style signing over order q?
options: s · k ≡ h + x · r (mod q)
r · k ≡ h + x · s (mod q)
s · x ≡ h + k · r (mod q)
h · k ≡ r + s · x (mod q)
questions.explanation: Rearranging the signature equation yields s·k ≡ h + x·r (mod q); if k repeats, you can solve for k and then x.

questions.question: RFC 6979 uses bits2int() when converting a hash to an integer. If the hash output is longer than qlen bits, what does bits2int() keep?
options: The rightmost qlen bits
The leftmost qlen bits
All bits (no truncation)
Only the middle qlen bits
questions.explanation: bits2int() keeps the leftmost qlen bits, matching how DSA/ECDSA interpret hash outputs relative to the group order bit length.

questions.question: In RFC 6979 nonce generation, what should you do if a generated candidate k is 0 or k ≥ q?
options: Clamp k into the range by taking k mod q and using it
Increment k by 1 until it is in range
Update the internal HMAC-DRBG state and try again
Abort signing because deterministic nonces cannot handle this case
questions.explanation: RFC 6979 specifies how to update (K,V) and continue generating candidates until 1 ≤ k < q.

questions.question: Two DSA signatures on different messages accidentally reused the same nonce k (so r repeats). Given h1, h2, s1, s2 (mod q), which formula recovers k?
questions.explanation: From s1·k ≡ h1 + x·r and s2·k ≡ h2 + x·r, subtract to get (s1-s2)·k ≡ (h1-h2) (mod q).

questions.question: Which statement about deterministic nonces (RFC 6979) is correct?
options: Deterministic nonces remove the need for private key randomness during key generation
Deterministic nonces guarantee the implementation is constant-time
Deterministic nonces make signatures compatible with standard DSA/ECDSA verifiers
Deterministic nonces allow reusing the same k safely across different messages
questions.explanation: RFC 6979 changes only how k is derived; the signature equations and verification remain standard and compatible.

questions.question: You switch the hash function from SHA-256 to SHA-512 but keep the same DSA private key x and the same message bytes. Under RFC 6979, what should happen to k?
options: k must stay identical because deterministic means hash-independent
k should usually change because the input h1 changes
k must become 0 for one of the hash functions
k should become unpredictable again, like a random nonce
questions.explanation: RFC 6979 is deterministic given (x, H(m)) under a specific hash function; changing the hash changes h1 and typically changes k.
